newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin foresees Russia, Belarus merger.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin foresees Russia, Belarus merger.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said on Wednesday he favours a complete merger of Russia with Belarus as the culmination of the integration process between the two Slav former Soviet republics.

"I think this will mean being very close," Yeltsin said in a rare interview shown on state-controlled Russian Television nine days before the planned signing of a charter to the Russia-Belarus union treaty signed last month.
"I think we will reach the point of being a single state," Yeltsin added.
Yeltsin and hardline Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko committed their countries to close integration in April 1996.
Exactly a year later, they signed amid heated public debates in both countries, a declaration containing their intention to build a two-state union.
Yeltsin and Lukashenko decided to put the charter of the new union up for public discussion before signing the details.
"On May 22 the final text of the charter will be handed over to the presidents," Yeltsin said. "We will lock ourselves in for a day or maybe less to polish the wording."
"The signing is on May 23," Yeltsin added resolutely.
However, he admitted that he and Lukashenko still disagreed on some issues including the ultimate aim of the union.
"The name of the future state is still to be decided," Yeltsin said. "It may be a federation, something we want, or some other option."
Sergei Shakhrai, a senior member of the Russian negotiating team, told NTV commercial television that the Belarus side had shown reluctance to allow too close a union.
"Russian delegations insist that the creation of a single federation is included in the document as the ultimate aim of the union," he said.
"The Belarus delegation and the Belarus president are resolutely opposed to any such inclusion," he added.
Lukashenko, who has made public in recent days his displeasure with the way negotiations were going, has pushed for equal status for himself and Belarus with Yeltsin and Russia.
Moscow appears set on making clear its size and relative wealth justify its claim to the senior role.

Opinion polls in Russia and Belarus have shown that the majority of population in both former Soviet republics favour closer ties or even merger. But different forces in both countries question the price of the Union.
Russian liberals warn Yeltsin against any deal with Lukashenko, whose authoritarian rule and bad human rights record have made him a pariah in the West.
Economic experts predict that Belarus, where economic reform is still in its embryonic phase, could slow Moscow's move toward capitalism and increase the difficulties of the Russian economy.
Nationalists in Belarus accuse Moscow of pursuing an imperialistic course and trying to end the independence won after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
About 3,000 people waving nationalist flags and carrying banners reading "Russia means war" protested in the Belarus capital minsk on Wednesday against plans for the union.
Yeltsin shrugged off objections. "I think it was a correct decision," he said.
